## Statistical inference {.title-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Week 6</div>

<div class="concept-line" style="margin-top:1em;">
How uncertain is our estimate — and how should we make decisions from data?
</div>

::: {.notes}
Week 5 gave us sampling distributions. Week 6 uses that machinery for estimation and decision-making. The entire lecture follows one randomized blood-pressure trial so the abstractions stay anchored.
:::

## We did everything correctly... right? {.motivation-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Opening case</div>

<div class="trial-pipeline fragment fade-up">
<div class="trial-step observed-border"><span>1</span><strong>Randomize</strong><small>placebo vs experimental</small></div>
<div class="trial-arrow">→</div>
<div class="trial-step observed-border"><span>2</span><strong>Blind</strong><small>reduce expectation bias</small></div>
<div class="trial-arrow">→</div>
<div class="trial-step observed-border"><span>3</span><strong>Measure</strong><small>systolic BP after treatment</small></div>
<div class="trial-arrow">→</div>
<div class="trial-step observed-border"><span>4</span><strong>Clean</strong><small>check data carefully</small></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Now we have numbers. What decision can they support?</div>
:::

## The observed result {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">A randomized two-arm trial</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">"Suppose we investigate new Drug $\text{A}$ as antihypertensive agent."</div>
:::

<div class="trial-summary fragment fade-up">
<div class="trial-summary-head">arm</div><div class="trial-summary-head">$n$</div><div class="trial-summary-head">mean SBP</div><div class="trial-summary-head">SD</div><div class="trial-summary-head">SE</div>
<div class="trial-arm placebo">placebo</div><div>80</div><div><strong>138.8</strong> mmHg</div><div>14.0</div><div>1.57</div>
<div class="trial-arm drug">experimental</div><div>80</div><div><strong>133.0</strong> mmHg</div><div>14.2</div><div>1.59</div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="w6-callout estimate-callout" style="font-size: 0.65em">Observed difference: <strong>$\hat\Delta = 133.0-138.8=-5.8$ mmHg</strong></div>
:::

::: {.notes}
The endpoint is deliberately incomplete: we are showing post-treatment BP without baseline BP. We return to that later.
:::

## Description is not yet inference {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">The transition</div>

<div class="w6-grid-3 fragment fade-up">
<div class="w6-card observed-border"><div class="w6-card-title">What we observed</div><div class="big-symbol observed">$-5.8$</div><div class="w6-card-sub">sample difference</div></div>
<div class="w6-card uncertainty-border"><div class="w6-card-title">What could vary</div><div class="big-symbol probability">$?$</div><div class="w6-card-sub">another random sample</div></div>
<div class="w6-card model-border"><div class="w6-card-title">What we want</div><div class="big-symbol model">$\Delta$</div><div class="w6-card-sub">population treatment effect</div></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Inference connects a noisy statistic to an unknown population quantity.</div>
:::

## And then someone asks for a yes/no answer {.motivation-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">The decision problem</div>

<div class="decision-stage fragment fade-up">
<div class="decision-data observed">data</div>
<div class="decision-arrow">→</div>
<div class="decision-uncertainty probability">uncertainty</div>
<div class="decision-arrow">→</div>
<div class="decision-action">action</div>
</div>

<div class="decision-question fragment fade-up">Should this result change what we do? (In this case market new Drug $\text{A}$)</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">Important</div><p>Statistics can quantify evidence and uncertainty. It cannot decide clinical value, ethics, benefit–risk, or regulatory policy by itself.</p></div>
:::

## Decision theory: data, actions, consequences {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">A minimal vocabulary</div>

<div class="decision-theory-grid fragment fade-up">
<div class="dt-node observed-border"><strong>State of nature</strong><span>what is actually true</span></div>
<div class="dt-node uncertainty-border"><strong>Data</strong><span>what the experiment reveals</span></div>
<div class="dt-node estimate-border"><strong>Decision rule</strong><span>how evidence maps to an action</span></div>
<div class="dt-node warning-border"><strong>Loss / consequence</strong><span>what errors cost us</span></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">A statistical rule is useful only in the context of consequences.</div>
:::

## Confidence interval {.section-break}

<div class="section-kicker">Part II</div>

<div class="section-title">The confidence interval</div>

<div class="section-subtitle">We now see how we can quantify the uncertainty of an estimate.</div>

## First: quantify uncertainty around an estimate {.section-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Confidence intervals</div>

<div class="section-equation">estimate $\pm$ uncertainty</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Week 5 already gave us the engine.</div>
:::

<div class="w6-flow-3 fragment fade-up">
<div class="w6-flow-node observed-border"><strong>sample mean</strong><span>$\bar X$ changes from sample to sample</span></div>
<div class="w6-flow-arrow">→</div>
<div class="w6-flow-node uncertainty-border"><strong>sampling distribution</strong><span>$\mathrm{SE}(\bar X)=\sigma/\sqrt n$</span></div>
<div class="w6-flow-arrow">→</div>
<div class="w6-flow-node model-border"><strong>population mean</strong><span>centered at $\mu$</span></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="definition-box"><div class="definition-title">Confidence interval</div><p>A procedure that uses the sampling distribution to construct a range of parameter values compatible with the observed estimate.</p></div>
:::

## The familiar 95% interval {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Normal-model intuition</div>

<div class="ci-formula-stage fragment fade-up">
<div class="ci-formula observed">$\bar x$</div>
<div class="ci-sign">$\pm$</div>
<div class="ci-formula probability">$1.96$</div>
<div class="ci-times">$\times$</div>
<div class="ci-formula uncertainty">$\mathrm{SE}(\bar X)$</div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">For a Normal model with known $\sigma$, this procedure covers $\mu$ in 95% of repeated samples.</div>
:::

::: {.notes}
More generally, critical values and standard errors depend on the model. Week 7 introduces t-based intervals and other specific tests.
:::

## Try it: confidence interval coverage {.exercise-slide}

<div class="try-label">Repeated-sampling laboratory · Normal population</div>

<div class="ci-widget" id="ciMeanWidget">
<div class="w6-control-grid ci-controls">
<label class="w6-control">population $\mu$ = <strong id="ciMuValue">0.0</strong><input id="ciMu" type="range" min="-5" max="5" value="0" step="0.5"></label>
<label class="w6-control">population $\sigma$ = <strong id="ciSigmaValue">2.0</strong><input id="ciSigma" type="range" min="0.5" max="5" value="2" step="0.5"></label>
<label class="w6-control">sample size $n$ = <strong id="ciNValue">20</strong><input id="ciN" type="range" min="5" max="200" value="20" step="5"></label>
<label class="w6-control">confidence = <strong id="ciLevelValue">95%</strong><input id="ciLevel" type="range" min="80" max="100" value="95" step="1"></label>
<label class="w6-control">interval type<select id="ciType"><option value="two">two-sided</option><option value="lower">lower bound</option><option value="upper">upper bound</option></select></label>
<label class="w6-control">repeated samples<select id="ciK"><option value="100">100</option><option value="500">500</option><option value="1000">1000</option></select></label>
<button id="ciRedraw" class="w6-button" type="button">Draw new samples</button>
<div class="w6-output"><span>empirical coverage</span><strong id="ciCoverage">—</strong></div>
</div>
<svg id="ciMeanSvg" class="w6-lab-svg ci-mean-svg" style="height:15em" viewBox="0 0 900 610" aria-label="Repeated confidence intervals and coverage"></svg>
</div>

## What should you notice? {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Coverage laboratory</div>

<div class="w6-grid-3 fragment fade-up">
<div class="w6-card uncertainty-border"><div class="w6-card-title">Increase $n$</div><div class="w6-card-sub">intervals get shorter because SE decreases</div></div>
<div class="w6-card estimate-border"><div class="w6-card-title">Keep 95%</div><div class="w6-card-sub">long-run coverage remains near 95%</div></div>
<div class="w6-card model-border"><div class="w6-card-title">Change $\sigma$</div><div class="w6-card-sub">more variable populations need wider intervals</div></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">Why no 100% confidence can be chosen?</div><p>For an unbounded Normal mean, guaranteed 100% coverage would require an interval extending without bound.</p></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="big-question">What does “95% confidence” mean?</div>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">Not this:</div><p>After the interval is calculated, the fixed population parameter is not “95% likely” to be inside this particular interval.</p></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">The 95% belongs to the long-run performance of the <strong>procedure</strong>.</div>
:::

## One-sided intervals use the same probability geometry {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Middle vs tail probability</div>

<div class="tail-grid fragment fade-up">

<div class="tail-card">
<div class="tail-title">two-sided</div>
<svg id="tailTwoSvg" class="tail-svg" style="height: 10em" viewBox="0 0 240 120" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"></svg>
<div class="tail-sub" style="font-size:80%">central $1-\alpha$</div>
</div>

<div class="tail-card">
<div class="tail-title">lower bound</div>
<svg id="tailLowerSvg" class="tail-svg" style="height: 10em" viewBox="0 0 240 120" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"></svg>
<div class="tail-sub" style="font-size:80%">protect against values below $L$</div>
</div>

<div class="tail-card">
<div class="tail-title">upper bound</div>
<svg id="tailUpperSvg" class="tail-svg" style="height: 10em" viewBox="0 0 240 120" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"></svg>
<div class="tail-sub" style="font-size:80%">protect against values above $U$</div>
</div>

</div>

## Proportions need intervals too {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Binary outcomes</div>

<div class="w6-grid-2 fragment fade-up">
<div class="w6-card observed-border"><div class="w6-card-title">Observed proportion</div><div class="big-symbol observed">$\hat p=x/n$</div><div class="w6-card-sub">e.g. response, toxicity, remission</div></div>
<div class="w6-card uncertainty-border"><div class="w6-card-title">Sampling uncertainty</div><div class="big-symbol probability">interval</div><div class="w6-card-sub">must respect the $0$ to $1$ boundary</div></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Same inferential idea; a different sampling model and interval formula.</div>
:::

## Try it: proportion confidence intervals {.exercise-slide}

<div class="try-label">Repeated-sampling laboratory · binary outcome</div>

<div class="ci-widget" id="ciPropWidget">
<div class="w6-control-grid prop-controls">
<label class="w6-control">population $p$ = <strong id="propPValue">0.30</strong><input id="propP" type="range" min="0.02" max="0.98" value="0.30" step="0.02"></label>
<label class="w6-control">sample size $n$ = <strong id="propNValue">40</strong><input id="propN" type="range" min="10" max="300" value="40" step="10"></label>
<label class="w6-control">confidence = <strong id="propLevelValue">95%</strong><input id="propLevel" type="range" min="80" max="99" value="95" step="1"></label>
<label class="w6-control">repeated samples<select id="propK"><option value="100">100</option><option value="500">500</option><option value="1000">1000</option></select></label>
<button id="propRedraw" class="w6-button" type="button">Draw new samples</button>
<div class="w6-output"><span>empirical coverage</span><strong id="propCoverage">—</strong></div>
</div>
<svg id="ciPropSvg" class="w6-lab-svg ci-prop-svg" style="height:15em" viewBox="0 0 900 610" aria-label="Repeated confidence intervals for a proportion"></svg>
</div>

::: {.notes}
The widget uses the Wilson interval. The method name is not the teaching target; the target is that binary sampling needs an interval suited to proportions, especially near 0 or 1.
:::

## Back to our trial: which interval matters? {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Two groups</div>

<div class="arm-ci-stage fragment fade-up">
<div class="arm-ci-row"><span class="arm-name placebo">placebo</span><div class="arm-track"><i style="left:42%;width:34%;"></i><b style="left:59%;"></b></div><span>138.8</span></div>
<div class="arm-ci-row"><span class="arm-name drug">experimental</span><div class="arm-track"><i style="left:14%;width:35%;"></i><b style="left:31%;"></b></div><span>133.0</span></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">Do not test a difference by eyeballing two separate CIs</div><p>Overlap of the two group intervals is not the formal criterion for whether the group means differ.</p></div>
:::

## Estimate the treatment effect directly {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">The contrast is the target</div>

<div class="effect-ci-stage fragment fade-up">
  <div class="effect-label">$\hat\Delta=-5.8$ mmHg · 95% CI approximately $[-10.2,-1.4]$</div>
  <div class="effect-track">
  <div class="effect-zero"></div>
  <div class="effect-interval"></div>
  <div class="effect-point"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="effect-axis"><span>−12</span><span>−8</span><span>−4</span><span>0</span><span>4</span></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">The interval asks the right question: which population differences are compatible with the observed difference?</div>
:::

## Significant is not the same as important {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Two different judgments</div>

<div class="significance-split fragment fade-up">
<div class="significance-card uncertainty-border"><div class="sig-question">Statistical</div><strong>Is the result difficult to explain by sampling variation under a reference model?</strong><span>statistics can help</span></div>
<div class="significance-card model-border"><div class="sig-question">Clinical / practical</div><strong>Is the magnitude large enough to matter for patients and decisions?</strong><span>requires domain context</span></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">A tiny effect can be statistically clear. A clinically valuable effect can remain uncertain in a small study.</div>
:::

## Hypothesis tests {.section-break}

<div class="section-kicker">Part III</div>

<div class="section-title">Hypothesis tests</div>

<div class="section-subtitle">We now see how we can devise a decision rule.</div>

## Now turn estimation into a decision rule {.section-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Hypothesis testing</div>

<div class="section-equation">assume a reference world → ask how unusual our statistic is</div>

## Scientific hypothesis ≠ statistical hypothesis {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Do not confuse the levels</div>

<div class="hypothesis-ladder fragment fade-up">
<div class="hyp-level science"><span>Scientific question</span><strong>Does the treatment improve cardiovascular health?</strong></div>
<div class="hyp-arrow">↓ operationalize</div>
<div class="hyp-level endpoint"><span>Clinical endpoint</span><strong>systolic blood pressure after treatment</strong></div>
<div class="hyp-arrow">↓ formalize</div>
<div class="hyp-level statistical"><span>Statistical hypothesis</span><strong>$H_0:\Delta=0$ versus an alternative</strong></div>
</div>

::: {.notes}
The statistical hypothesis is narrower than the scientific claim. Rejecting a BP null hypothesis does not prove the full clinical hypothesis.
:::

## Step 1: define the null reference {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">A specific parameter statement</div>

<div class="hypothesis-pair fragment fade-up">
<div class="hyp-card null"><span>Null</span><strong>$H_0:\Delta=0$</strong><small>no population mean difference in this example</small></div>
<div class="hyp-card alt"><span>Alternative</span><strong>$H_1:\Delta\ne0$</strong><small>population means differ</small></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">Not always “no difference”</div><p>Equivalence and non-inferiority questions use different null hypotheses. We meet them next week.</p></div>
:::

## Step 2: choose the direction before seeing the result {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Alternative hypotheses</div>

<div class="alt-grid fragment fade-up">
<div class="alt-card"><div class="alt-symbol">$\Delta\ne0$</div><strong>two-sided</strong><span>either direction matters</span></div>
<div class="alt-card"><div class="alt-symbol">$\Delta<0$</div><strong>lower-tail</strong><span>only sufficiently lower values count</span></div>
<div class="alt-card"><div class="alt-symbol">$\Delta>0$</div><strong>upper-tail</strong><span>only sufficiently higher values count</span></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Direction is a design choice, not something to choose after inspecting the data.</div>
:::

## Step 3: standardize the observed discrepancy {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Test statistic</div>

<div class="test-stat-stage fragment fade-up">
<div class="test-stat-numerator">observed effect − null effect</div>
<div class="test-stat-bar"></div>
<div class="test-stat-denominator">standard error</div>
<div class="test-stat-equals">$=\;z$</div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">A good test statistic transforms the problem into a reference distribution we understand.</div>
:::

## The null world is a counterfactual model {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">If $H_0$ were true...</div>

<div class="null-world fragment fade-up">

<svg
  id="nullWorldSvg"
  viewBox="0 0 820 310"
  class="null-svg"
  preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"
  aria-label="Standard normal null distribution with central 95 percent region">
</svg>

</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">With $\alpha=0.05$, sufficiently extreme statistics fall in the rejection region.</div>
:::

## Step 4: compare the statistic with the null world {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Our trial</div>

<div class="observed-z fragment fade-up">
<div class="z-number">$z\approx -2.6$</div>
<div class="z-track"><span class="z-reject-left">reject</span><i class="z-bound-left"></i><b class="z-zero"></b><i class="z-bound-right"></i><span class="z-reject-right">reject</span><em class="z-observed"></em></div>
<div class="z-scale"><span>−4</span><span>−1.96</span><span>0</span><span>+1.96</span><span>+4</span></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">The observed standardized difference lies in a region that is uncommon under $H_0$.</div>
:::

## Step 5: summarize extremeness with a p-value {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">A tail probability under $H_0$</div>

<div class="definition-box fragment fade-up">
<div class="definition-title">p-value</div>
<p>Assuming the null hypothesis and the statistical model are correct, the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one.</p>
</div>

<div class="pvalue-equation fragment fade-up">our illustrative trial: $p\approx0.009$</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">It is not</div><p>the probability that $H_0$ is true, nor the probability that the result happened “by chance.”</p></div>
:::

## A small p-value is evidence against the reference model {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">But evidence is not effect size</div>

<div class="pvalue-split fragment fade-up">
<div class="pvalue-card"><span>p-value</span><strong>compatibility with $H_0$</strong><small>depends strongly on sample size and precision</small></div>
<div class="pvalue-card"><span>effect estimate</span><strong>magnitude + direction</strong><small>answers how much, in the observed scale</small></div>
<div class="pvalue-card"><span>confidence interval</span><strong>precision</strong><small>shows a range of compatible effect values</small></div>
</div>

## Where does $\alpha=0.05$ enter? {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">A pre-specified decision threshold</div>

<div class="alpha-stage fragment fade-up">
<div class="alpha-card probability"><span>significance level</span><strong>$\alpha$</strong><small>long-run Type I error target under Null</small></div>
<div class="alpha-arrow">→</div>
<div class="alpha-card"><span>decision rule</span><strong>reject if $p<\alpha$</strong><small>for the chosen testing procedure</small></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">$0.05$ is a convention, not a law of nature</div><p>The threshold should be pre-specified and justified by the scientific and decision context.</p></div>
:::

## CI and hypothesis test are two views of the same machinery {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">For matching two-sided procedures</div>

<div class="duality-stage fragment fade-up">
<div class="duality-ci"><span>95% CI for $\Delta$</span><div class="duality-track"><i></i><b></b></div><small>does not include 0</small></div>
<div class="duality-equals">⇔</div>
<div class="duality-test"><span>two-sided test at $\alpha=0.05$</span><strong>reject $H_0:\Delta=0$</strong></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">The interval usually tells us more because it also shows direction and plausible magnitude.</div>
:::

## Hypothesis testing workflow {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">A repeatable sequence</div>

<div class="workflow-5 fragment fade-up">
<div><span>1</span><strong>Define</strong><small>parameter + null hypothesis</small></div>
<div><span>2</span><strong>Choose</strong><small>test statistic + assumptions</small></div>
<div><span>3</span><strong>Calculate</strong><small>statistic + SE</small></div>
<div><span>4</span><strong>Reference</strong><small>null distribution + p-value</small></div>
<div><span>5</span><strong>Interpret</strong><small>effect + CI + context</small></div>
</div>

## Try it: repeat the drug trial {.exercise-slide}

<div class="try-label">Same population effect · new random trial</div>

<div class="trial-widget" id="trialWidget">
<div class="w6-control-grid trial-controls">
<label class="w6-control">patients per arm $n$ = <strong id="trialNValue">80</strong><input id="trialN" type="range" min="20" max="300" value="80" step="10"></label>
<button id="trialRedraw" class="w6-button" type="button">Run a new trial</button>
<div class="w6-output" style="font-size: 1.2em"><span>true Δ</span><strong>−6.0 mmHg</strong></div>
<div class="w6-output" style="font-size: 1.2em"><span>common σ</span><strong>14 mmHg</strong></div>
</div>
<div class="trial-widget-grid">
<div class="trial-widget-panel"><div class="mini-title">observed arm means</div><svg id="trialMeansSvg" viewBox="0 0 420 250"></svg></div>
<div class="trial-widget-panel"><div class="mini-title">estimated treatment effect</div><svg id="trialEffectSvg" viewBox="0 0 420 250"></svg></div>
</div>
<div class="trial-results">
<div><span style="font-size: 1.3em">$\hat\Delta$</span><strong id="trialDelta">—</strong></div>
<div><span>95% CI</span><strong id="trialCI">—</strong></div>
<div><span>p-value</span><strong id="trialP">—</strong></div>
<div><span>standardized effect</span><strong id="trialD">—</strong></div>
</div>
</div>

## What changes when $n$ changes? {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Precision is not magnitude</div>

<div class="n-effect-grid fragment fade-up">
<div class="n-effect-card"><span>$n\uparrow$</span><strong>$\mathrm{SE}\downarrow$</strong><small>sampling distribution narrows</small></div>
<div class="n-effect-card"><span>$n\uparrow$</span><strong>CI narrows</strong><small>estimate becomes more precise</small></div>
<div class="n-effect-card"><span>$n\uparrow$</span><strong>p can shrink</strong><small>same-size effects become easier to detect</small></div>
<div class="n-effect-card"><span>$n\uparrow$</span><strong>true effect unchanged</strong><small>biology did not become stronger</small></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">This is why “statistically significant” cannot substitute for “important.”</div>
:::

## Effect size asks “how much?” {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Magnitude on different scales</div>

<div class="effect-size-grid fragment fade-up">
  <div class="effect-size-card observed-border">
  <span>RAW EFFECT</span>
  <strong>$\hat\Delta = \bar{x}_T - \bar{x}_C$</strong>
  <small>mmHg · often easiest to interpret clinically</small>
  </div>
  <div class="effect-size-card estimate-border">
  <span>STANDARDIZED EFFECT</span>
  <strong>$d = \frac{\bar{x}_T - \bar{x}_C}{s_{\mathrm{pooled}}}$</strong>
  <small>difference expressed in SD units</small>
  </div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">Standardized ≠ automatically meaningful</div><p>Clinical relevance still needs a domain-specific threshold and benefit–risk context.</p></div>
:::

## We hid something important in our endpoint {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Baseline blood pressure</div>

<div class="baseline-stage fragment fade-up">
<div class="baseline-arm placebo"><strong>placebo</strong><span>baseline ?</span><span>post 138.8</span></div>
<div class="baseline-arm drug"><strong>experimental</strong><span>baseline ?</span><span>post 133.0</span></div>
<div class="baseline-question">Were the groups starting from the same place?<br>Should we compare absolute or fold change relative to baseline?</div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Randomization balances baseline variables <strong>in expectation</strong>, not perfectly in every realized trial.</div>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">Analysis consequence</div><p>Baseline should be measured and handled according to the pre-specified design—for example with change from baseline or baseline-adjusted analysis. A post-treatment mean alone can hide important context.</p></div>
:::

## Decisions create two kinds of errors {.section-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Type I, Type II, power</div>

<div class="section-equation">reality × decision</div>

<div class="decision-matrix fragment fade-up">
<div class="matrix-empty"></div><div class="matrix-head">$H_0$ world</div><div class="matrix-head">$H_1$ world</div>
<div class="matrix-side">do not reject $H_0$</div><div class="matrix-good">correct<br><small style="font-size: 1.2em">$1-\alpha$</small></div><div class="matrix-beta"><strong>Type II error</strong><span>$\beta$</span></div>
<div class="matrix-side">reject $H_0$</div><div class="matrix-alpha"><strong>Type I error</strong><span>$\alpha$</span></div><div class="matrix-good">correct<br><small style="font-size: 1.2em">$\text{power}=1-\beta$</small></div>
</div>

## Type I error: false positive {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Rejecting a true null</div>

<div class="error-story fragment fade-up">
<div class="error-world model">no real treatment effect</div>
<div class="error-arrow">→</div>
<div class="error-data observed">an unusually favorable sample</div>
<div class="error-arrow">→</div>
<div class="error-decision warning">we reject $H_0$</div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">The significance level $\alpha$ controls this long-run error probability for the specified test.</div>
:::

## Type II error: false negative {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Missing a real effect</div>

<div class="error-story fragment fade-up">
<div class="error-world estimate">a real treatment effect exists</div>
<div class="error-arrow">→</div>
<div class="error-data observed">a noisy or underpowered sample</div>
<div class="error-arrow">→</div>
<div class="error-decision probability">we do not reject $H_0$</div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="definition-box"><div class="definition-title">Power</div><p>$1-\beta$: probability that the procedure rejects $H_0$ when a specified alternative effect is truly present.</p></div>
:::

## Which error is worse? {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">There is no universal answer</div>

<div class="risk-grid fragment fade-up">
<div class="risk-card warning-border"><strong>False positive</strong><span>approve an ineffective or harmful intervention</span><small>patient safety · cost · trust</small></div>
<div class="risk-card uncertainty-border"><strong>False negative</strong><span>discard an actually useful intervention</span><small>missed benefit · lost investment · delayed care</small></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Design is a balance among error rates, meaningful effect sizes, feasibility, and consequences.</div>
:::

## What controls power? {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Make the two worlds easier to distinguish</div>

<div class="power-grid fragment fade-up">
<div class="power-card"><strong>bigger true effect</strong><span style="font-size: 120%">$|\Delta_1-\Delta_0|\uparrow$</span><small>worlds separate</small></div>
<div class="power-card"><strong>larger sample</strong><span style="font-size: 120%">$n\uparrow$</span><small>SE shrinks</small></div>
<div class="power-card"><strong>less variability</strong><span style="font-size: 120%">$\sigma\downarrow$</span><small>curves narrow</small></div>
<div class="power-card"><strong>larger<span style="font-size: 140%">$\alpha$</span></strong><span>easier rejection</span><small>but more Type I error</small></div>
</div>

## Two important concepts {.concept-slide}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Power depends on a specified alternative.</div>
<div class="definition-box">Sample-size planning therefore needs an effect size worth detecting—not just an arbitrary desire for “80% power.”</div>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Non-significant does not mean equivalent.</div>
<div class="warning-box"><div class="warning-title">$p\ge\alpha$ means</div><p>we did not obtain enough evidence to reject this null with this procedure. It does <strong>not</strong> prove that the populations are equivalent.</p></div>
:::

## One test is manageable. What about many? {.section-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Multiplicity</div>

<div class="section-equation">more opportunities to be fooled</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Repeating tests creates more false-positive opportunities.</div>
:::

<div class="multiplicity-dots fragment fade-up">
<div class="test-dot">1</div><div class="test-dot">2</div><div class="test-dot">3</div><div class="test-dot">4</div><div class="test-dot">5</div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="multiplicity-equation">If five tests were independent and each used $\alpha=0.05$:</div>
<div class="multiplicity-big">$\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one Type I error})=1-(1-0.05)^5\approx22.6\%$</div>
<div class="concept-line fade-up">This is assuming every null is true.</div>
:::

::: {.notes}
The formula assumes independent tests. Correlated endpoints change the exact family-wise probability; the general multiplicity problem remains.
:::

## Multiplicity correction changes the decision rule {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Different goals, different procedures</div>

<div class="correction-grid fragment fade-up">
<div class="correction-card"><strong>Bonferroni</strong><span>simple, conservative</span><small>controls family-wise error</small></div>
<div class="correction-card"><strong>Holm</strong><span>step-down procedure</span><small>controls family-wise error</small></div>
<div class="correction-card"><strong>FDR methods</strong><span>e.g. Benjamini–Hochberg</span><small>control expected false-discovery proportion</small></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Stricter Type I error control usually costs power. Multiplicity is another decision trade-off.</div>
:::

## The famous dead-salmon lesson {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Many comparisons can manufacture discoveries</div>

<div class="salmon-card fade-up">
  <img src="figures/salmon.jpg" alt="Dead Salmon" class="salmon-img">
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">The point is not that imaging is unreliable—the point is that large families of tests require explicit error control.</div>

## Misconception check {.exercise-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Decide before revealing</div>

<div class="quiz-grid">
<div class="quiz-card fragment fade-up"><strong>“$p=0.03$ means there is a 97% chance the treatment works.”</strong><div class="quiz-answer is-false fragment fade-in">False · p is calculated assuming $H_0$.</div></div>
<div class="quiz-card fragment fade-up"><strong>“A 95% CI gives the plausible effect magnitude, not just a yes/no answer.”</strong><div class="quiz-answer fragment fade-in">Yes · that is one reason intervals are so useful.</div></div>
<div class="quiz-card fragment fade-up"><strong>“If $p=0.20$, we proved there is no effect.”</strong><div class="quiz-answer is-false fragment fade-in">False · failure to reject is not proof of equivalence.</div></div>
<div class="quiz-card fragment fade-up"><strong>“With a huge $n$, a tiny effect may become statistically significant.”</strong><div class="quiz-answer fragment fade-in">Yes · precision increases with sample size.</div></div>
</div>

## Would you trust this conclusion? {.exercise-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">Inference needs more than a p-value</div>

<div class="trust-case fragment fade-up">
<div class="trust-result"><span>Effect</span><strong>−1.2 mmHg</strong></div>
<div class="trust-result"><span>95% CI</span><strong>[−1.5, −0.9]</strong></div>
<div class="trust-result"><span>p-value</span><strong>&lt; 0.001</strong></div>
<div class="trust-result"><span style="font-size: 110%">$n$</span><strong>20,000</strong></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="question-line" style="font-size: 110%">Statistically significant? <strong>Yes.</strong></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="question-line" style="font-size: 110%">Clinically important? <strong>We still need a clinical threshold.</strong></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="question-line" style="font-size: 110%">Trustworthy? <strong>Only after checking design, endpoint, assumptions, missingness, multiplicity, and bias.</strong></div>
:::

## Week 6 synthesis {.concept-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">From sample to decision</div>

<div class="synthesis-flow fragment fade-up">
<div class="synth-node observed-border"><strong>estimate</strong><span>what did we observe?</span></div>
<div class="synth-arrow">→</div>
<div class="synth-node uncertainty-border"><strong>SE + sampling distribution</strong><span>how much would it vary?</span></div>
<div class="synth-arrow">→</div>
<div class="synth-node estimate-border"><strong>CI + effect size</strong><span>how much and how precise?</span></div>
<div class="synth-arrow">→</div>
<div class="synth-node probability-border"><strong>test + p-value</strong><span>compatibility with</span><span style="font-size: 110%">$H_0$</span></div>
<div class="synth-arrow">→</div>
<div class="synth-node warning-border"><strong>decision</strong><span>errors + consequences + context</span></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
<div class="concept-line">Inference is not a single number. It is a structured argument from data under uncertainty.</div>
:::
